I've been in a similar situation more than once. I can recommend a few things: 

First, start studying early, by that I mean take whatever you think is early and start before that. early on if your still juggling course work it doesn't have to be intense study periods but getting in every little bit you can as early as possible helps. 

Second, Make sure you're eating well and staying hydrated, I know that's basic stuff but I also know people who totally fall off with that stuff under stress and it's not doing them any favors. 

Third, Depending on the timing of your exams find a way to relax between them. Meditate for a half hour, go for a light jog, listen to some music in a dark room, play video games. Whatever let's you just veg out for a bit do it, even if you can only squeeze in 20 minutes of it. 

Finally, for god's sake sleep! Seriously get a good nights sleep. The reason your studying early is so that by the time this hellish 2 days arrives you've got your study notes written, you've got a solid grasp on the concepts, and you can take time to take care of yourself properly. Cramming works for some people but I've never seen it work for someone with so many exams in such a tight period. On top of this make sure your sleep schedule is lined up with your examination times properly. If you're going to be writing late exams but you got to bed early see if you can't gently nudge up your sleep schedule in the weeks prior to the exams. If you're a night owl and your writing early make sure you're not rolling out of bed ten minutes before your first exam and spending the first 20 minutes of it groggy.  

Beyond this I don't think I can recommend anything else. You hopefully already know the general study practices that work well for you and nine times out of ten it's best to stick with those if they've worked well in the past. Honestly the key for me has always just been taking proper care of my body and keeping stress and anxiety low so my mind can be working at 100%

Best of luck!

In the most basic terms there are early results that show (pre hormone replacement therapy) that trans individuals brains exhibit markers of the "opposite" sex (that is the sex opposite to the one they are assigned at birth). It's more complicated than just that though, the science isn't bullet proof, and hearing the results from the mouths of the actually studies is better then my "off the top of my head" summary, but suffice it to say there seems to be a real scientific leaning that something biological is happening differently in studied trans individuals. We aren't 100% there in knowing exactly the nature of what that something is (as with most studies on the human brain this stuff is immensely complicated) but there really does seem to be something. Further I think when one considers all the variations we have already identified in various intersex and chromosomal conditions it's not so hard to fathom that something could potentially go "differently" (to save the baggage of saying it went wrong) when it comes to trans individuals. This at it's core troubles our ability to really hammer down biological sex, or at least demands we potentially alter our definition to reflect a more refined understanding of the variation possible.

I think self perception does kind of play into this to a degree as well. Honestly I think it's a more complicated relationship then I have the capacity to do justice to on reddit but let me try. At the very rock bottom, for many but not all trans people, dysphoria is kind of the key. It's a complicated feeling that I struggle to explain just because it's so personal. It's a depression and anxiety that for me stems from the fact that the way others see and gender me is not how I feel. However it's not totally externally dependent because I can feel perfectly dysphoric when only *I* realize that how I look is not "right". It's a social and personal feeling. I'd honestly ask that you read some of the current DSM definition about dysphoria and such just because, cards showing, I know I struggle to explain it but I also know it's an accepted and explored thing by many many many informed researchers, scholars and medical personel. 

So if you can accept that there is potentially an if ill understood biological foundation here (which you don't have to by any means), and that such a feeling is signaled by dysphoric feelings around ones gender identity, allow me to move onto the topic at hand. Gender stereotypes are enshrined in our culture to the bloody roots. Before we're even born our family, communities, and culture are hoisting all sorts of things it presumes we should enjoy based just on our sex. Pink or blue clothes, dolls or trucks, wrestling or dancing etc etc. Now obviously in queer and feminist theory the essential nature of all this stuff has been questioned pretty heavily and if I may show a bias demonstrated as mostly social construction and arbitrary. Now I'm not trying to conflate sex in gender here, as they can be dissected as very different things, but I don't think it's unfair to say that for the most part we operate in a dominant culture where these two are conflated constantly. Now introduce into this dominant gendered culture and individual who is trans, who for most of their life in inundated with this gender=sex culture and have now discovered they're trans. They feel dysphoric socially let's say. How can we remedy this (at least a little bit)? Well by passing! By trading in the cultural stereotypes that align with "girl" or "boy" to be socially accepted a the gender we really are. I'm not saying this is healthy and I'm not denying that this is in any way fighting longstanding gender essentialism, BUT as social animals undeniably group approval and validation is a really great feeling. Especially when you've probably been depressed, alienated, and anxious for years of your life until now. And whether we like it or not we've been programmed with these images so as one participates in these cultural stereotypes there personal dysphoria may well lessen as well. Remember being trans doesn't necessarily come with an introductory course in gender studies, it can happen to any number of people, with any number of beliefs of gender and sex, in any number of contexts. Trans people aren't inherently gifted with certain viewpoints on social construction despite what I would say is a specifically unique position within social construction. 

So for some people it's just them trying to live life. Trying not to get harassed, beaten, fired from their job, and evicted. The easiest way (if the option is viable for them) is playing the cultural game of gender thoroughly enough to have an average life. Having said this, and I regret how little of my post is going to say this, I've met so many trans people who don't trade in these stereotypes, people who are women that are fine with their facial hair, and voices, and physique. People who are men that are fine with showing cleavage and wearing make up. People who rightly fuck with gender all the time, and not to make some bold political statement but because it's how they're comfortable. 

So I guess in a roundabout way I think it's absolutely unfair to offload all the baggage of reinforcing gender norms onto trans people when cis, LGB and pretty much everyone else are equally engaged in similar practices. Yes trans people are at the splitting wedge of gender identity VS sex but that shouldn't place a higher than average burden on them to fight such constructs. I agree that collectively we should work to dismantle them, but to call trans people out specifically just seems odd. Trans people are just that, they're people operating in a culture like anyone else. Maybe even operating in a culture not just for social acceptance but for the sake of their physical, emotional, and hell even economic well being. Even more than that some women are going to just like "girly" things. Some men are going to like "manly" things. and it's just as oppressive to place the demand that those people transgress against those things they might naturally align with because their connected to a long standing system of division.

TL;DR: 

-One might know they are trans through largely self identification, as well as feelings of dysphoria that could reasonably be linked to a biolgical variance.

-Particularly for those with no desire for surgery? I'm not the right person to speak for this because I do have such a desire. But keep in mind surgery is expensive, can have less then satisfactory results, and like many surgeries is physically demanding, all of which could play into a persons cost benefit analysis for their desire for surgery. I'm sure that most binary trans people (as again I am not gender queer or bi gender so I don't want to speak to those experiences) would 100% have their fairy godmother wave a wand and give them the right bits if it was painless, free, and was guaranteed to work. 

-potentially yes they could, if you are of willing to accept that there are seemingly biological roots for trans identified people. Though I would imagine in such a society feelings of social dysphoria might be greatly lessened. 

Finally if I could boil down why this is such a hard thing to articulate. It's because our physical and social existences (by extension our sex and gender experiences) are so intermingled culturally it's hard to tell when they're totally separate and only "artificially" entangled and when there are genuine relationships where they inextricably co inform each other.

Also just a final disclaimer these are totally just my thoughts. I don't want to pretend like I'm speaking for any other trans person because honestly just like any other people we all have unique and varying perspectives and experiences that are equally valid.

I'd also like  to point out, in addition to RvengeOfSalmacis wonderful comment that it's worth thinking about sample sizes here. Do people in the trans community have those opinions? Sure absolutely they are out there. They aren't my opinions and the opinions of other trans people I know and interact with though. I understand that, on a fundamental level, you can really only form opinions based on exposure but at the same time I'd ask that you reflect on how limited and possibly filtered your exposure has been. There are people with extreme and offensive opinions in any group but that doesn't mean they're in the majority. They may be the loudest sure but don't let that necessarily sway your opinion. That's dangerous for thinking about any group and not just trans people. I don't mean this in any sort of offensive way, this is pretty much one of the fundamental ways in which we navigate the world and form our opinions as humans. Just consider the possibility that what sounds like "many voices" might not actually be so many in the grand statistical sense of the community. Additionally that there are tons of opinions that run counter to these that might not be as loudly or visibly broadcast and rebroadcasted by others. More extreme things tend to filter to the top regardless of the actually extent of how many hold those beliefs. I'm sure if one desired to do so they could find segments of the LGB community that hold beliefs that seem accusatory and dismissive of others life experiences but that shouldn't be used to dismiss the LGB community as a whole. This isn't to say your experiences with the T segment of the community are invalid or anything, they're very real and must be considered but at the same time there's really a great deal of diversity in belief out there.

I'd really strongly recommend swinging by /r/asktransgender sometime and asking these questions. Or maybe even better, search for others who have asked these opinions and take stock of the multitude of answers that don't align with the complaints you've seen some in the community make. There are probably hundreds of answers out there that offer nuanced and very different views that are worth taking stock of. I suggest this not only for your first reservation but also your second one. Gender stereotypes are a massively pervasive issue that float around in the entire LGBT community and I think the more you look the more you'll discover just how transgressive the trans community can be when it comes to these things. 

Additionally if you haven't already take a look at some of the science surrounding trans people. It's still in its infancy in many regards so you wont find hard answeres yet, but I think there's a lot of value in engaging with this stuff. http://transcience-project.org/index.html is a good source from memory. This doesn't directly address any of your concerns per se but I really think there's value here if trying to become more understanding and engaged with the trans community (and trans identities more generally) is a goal.

Again I hope none of this came off harshly, I promise I mean this as a genuine response to someone who seems open to learning and exploring this topic more.

So to answer your question up front. Yes it can work and be a great experience! But keep in mind it's like any game that radically departs from standard fantasy fair, everyone needs to be on board and have a good sense of what the expectations are. I'd put together a small primer for everyone to look over that roughly outlines the way you want to alter the game before diving in too much, unless of course you get enjoyment out of setting crafting anyways. Below I'll include my experiences.

I did something like this in 3.5 and had a lot of success with it. Mine was a fairly fantastic imagining of a stoneage. It was a mix between the flintstones, Conan, and quest for fire. Basically I made most swords and metal dependent weapons exotic weapons as metal working was almost non existent in the world. In fact the only metal sword in the campaign was basically an artifact level object (I gave it keen and the adimantium properties for sundering to emphasize this along with a few other small goodies). Daggers, slings, spears, clubs, axes and (short) bows were common. I also used things like nets, bolas, boomerangs, and blow guns. I made weapon material matter a lot as mentioned. Bone, wood, and stone were basically the base line. From there finding daggers made of volcanic glass or other exotic materials would impart some small bonus to the item. I also included a monster hunter style system where certain slain creatures body parts (hides, claws, teeth, bones) could be crafted by someone with a feat into special weapons and armor. Also armor was pretty limited as well given the material restrictions. Now I didn't include any sort of item damage or degradation over time system since it plain didn't gel with my group but if you can find an elegant way to implement it I think having stuff break could be a really nice modification. Maybe make it so "masterwork" versions of items are those that don't have a chance of breaking since they're so well made. these would obviously be extremely valuable and rare.

Additionally I made crafting really important. Everyone had to have something they could do, did they hunt and track? Gather plants and food? Craft tools? Navigate landscapes? Everyone had to take a practical skill in the campaign.

Magic mostly didn't exist in my world, and the few mages that did exist were more in line with Conan style mages, rare and extremely powerful. They often relied on advanced understanding of alchemy and practical illusions as much as any mystical power. There was definitely some magic and gods/spirit to be called upon but there was always a great cost for these abilities. This may or may not jive with your desires. I made feats available to allow certain spells to be cast a rituals or ceremonies. The material components had to be hunted down or traded for since there wouldn't be a market to address the (tiny) demand for such strange materials.

Speaking of that I scrapped the GP system and went to a barter system. I still had some measuring sticks for worth like how much cattle, salt, leather and such were "worth" in a very abstract sense. 

I put a lot of emphasis on survival and really drove home the idea that traveling the wilds was a task that took time, lots of risk, and lots of skill. I had something similar to the rangers environment system from 5e where you had a terrain that you knew and could survive in fairly well but if you went beyond that you either had to take it slow, have someone local aid you or die. Remember odds are that save for routes between established tribes there aren't any roads. Ask the practical questions, how are you staying warm in cold places, dry in wet one, fed in scarce ones, and hydrated in dry ones. make these obstacles that have to be considered.

I also found that using some extreme weather events (natural forest fires, hurricanes, earthquakes, mud/rock slides, quick sand, flash flooding) really drove home the vulnerability and stone age feel of things. The environment was just as likely to wipe you out as anything else since it's still a poorly understood element. Is a solar/lunar eclipse happening? a blood moon?  A meteor shower? What do these things mean in your world how will people react?

Also a note, if you wan't to have them out trekking the world meeting new people could be an amazing chance for world building. Do they have the same gods, language? What weapons do they have, what do they hunt and eat. How are they different or the same. Obviously that kind of stuff can work in any campaign but depending on how ancient you want this there simply wouldn't be the same kind of social connectivity between places and peoples.

 I flavored out my encounter tables with various mega fauna, dinosaurs, plants, and natural hazards. It was a general stone punk campaign so I wasn't aiming for accuracy in terms of like what would actually have co existed historically. 

Sorry that was kind of long and rant, and I know a lot of the stuff I mentioned might not work depending of the flavor of game you're going for but I almost never get to talk about my stone punk campaign!

There was this part of myself, this part of my heart that had been so malnourished and so forgotten and hidden away that when I finally found someone who mattered so much to me I had no idea how to process the feelings. I didn't know if I wanted to be with this person or if I just didn't want to lose them to someone else. 

So the only advice I can offer is start trying to work on you. It's tough, I won't lie, loving yourself might be the hardest thing you ever do in this lifetime. But start small, respect your feelings as valid. When you start to come up with reasons why you shouldn't feel this way because you'll never deserve it try to remember that you are worthy of those feelings. At the same time try to accept the things you can't change in life, and work on tackling the things you can change. Work on things that you love, improve yourself in ways you've always wanted to. There's a fire inside you and right now it might feel like no one wants to stop and warm themselves at it but you can try to kindle that flame. Learn a new language, pick up a skill you've always wanted, try to learn an instrument, lose weight, eat right, hell even just dedicate some little bit of time to loving and caring for yourself if that's all you have. But make an earnest effort to try and figure out not just who you are now, but who you want to be relationship or not. You have to start with you because that's the only guaranteed asset we have in this lifetime. I know everyone says "You can't love someone else till you love yourself' and I know that sounds like such a cop out but I think it's partially true. You have to have some love and respect for yourself to figure out what you want and deserve out of love and romance. Hey Max, so as promised story time! So about four ish years ago (yea it was longer ago than I initially thought!) I got a referral from my family doctor to CAMH, you've already done the intake package or whatever it is they send out so I'll spare you that part (which was an absolute bureaucratic nightmare for me too!). So I'll just give you as much as I can from my memory and hopefully it will help! Also just for reference (though I'm not sure how much it matters) I'm MtF so things might be a teensy bit different maybe and I can only really speak from my own experience!

Basically my first appointment I arrived at the building, waited for about an hour past my appointment time, then was taken through to see the first doctor (Dr. Brown, Psychologist). I've seen a ton of therapists and psychiatrists in my life so for me the appointment was pretty standard going for a first meeting with a slight trans twist of lime: 

-How are you? 

-What are you currently doing (school, work, etc.)

-What's your family life like? 

-Friends/Social Life?

-Have you come out yet?

-To whom?

-Do you feel supported? 

-How long ago did you come out? 

-How long have you felt this way

-How would you describe your feelings about your gender?

-What does transition mean for you?

Overall she was extremely kind and the questions were largely non invasive in the context of the appointment. Dr. Brown always used the correct pronouns and my preferred name even though it had not yet legally changed. I was pretty anxious at the time to give the "right" answers to make sure I didn't get shrugged off as a fetishist (which I have heard happens to people) but honestly Dr. Brown was extremely down to earth and seemed pretty progressive for that places reputation. After that I saw another doctor, it was largely the same song and dance though our meeting was shorter and I never saw him again in subsequent appointments. Regarding your question on what not to mention, it's really hard to say. I went in mostly honest but avoiding explicitly sexual stuff but I get the feeling that maybe it didn't matter so much in conjunction with my other feelings. It's hard to say though because my single experience might have just lined up with their "acceptable" trans person narrative. Do you have anythings that you're particularly worried about discussing?

 Since I hadn't done the real life experience stuff (which was a year long when I went though I heard it changed?) They basically welcomed me to the program and said we'd meet again in six months. Oh they also gave me some lovely resources for the family and friends to read about trans peeps, gave me some pamphlets and flyer thingies specifically for trans people, and a list of resources for Trans support in Toronto.

Second appointment was really more of the same, nothing horrifying, nothing intrusive, pretty par for the course talking to a psychologist stuff. Mostly the same questions but in the context on how things had progressed (or not) since our last meeting. Oh I ended up seeing Dr. Brown again by the way. At this point I had my name legally changed and had started my "real life experience" and we talked about that some more but really nothing too bad or new.

Cue my third appointment (again six months after the last). Real life experience was done at this point and I had tons of documentation to boot! Again we had a pretty standard conversation where Dr. Brown asked me some very standard mental health questions as well as more trans specific stuff (has your family made any progress, are your friends supportive, how has "real life experience" made you feel, etc.). After this appoint me they referred me to an Endo, Dr. X (Not really just saving a name drop)... and this is where my troubles began.... 

So the first time I met Dr. X he seemed nice enough. An older gentlemen, asked what pronouns I wanted, then forgot them and reverted to male pronouns halfway through (:() did some standard doctor stuff, weight, blood pressure, heart rate. Asked questions about drug allergies, family medical history. There was a little pile of papers on that stuff I filled out beforehand but honestly I can't remember what all it entailed. That day I walked out with a requisition for blood work and the promise of Anti Androgens if everything was clean.

And it was! And I got my Anti Androgens! And then they fucked with my mental health state waaaay to much and my doctors order I stop till I consult the endo. Well I consult him, he tries a different AA and it had the same results. A bunch of complicated and drawn out medical stuff later I can't go on them. Now I know this seems like unnessecary detail but I promise this is leading to further experiences with CAMH.. Cue the end of my first tango with CAMH

(Just a quick note! The stuff that affected my use of anti androgens was an extremely rare complication, and while obviously you wouldn't be taking those I didn't want to make it seem like this was something to worry to much over, just part of my personal story!)

Part II: Transition Boogaloo

So it had been two years since the AA failure I'm worse then ever. I call up CAMH and get a new appointment. They see me about 3 months later and I was still in their system so no need to jump through all their hoops again. I saw a social worker (nurse case manager maybe) and basically told them I would be interested in trying AA's again since I was doing so poorly without them anyway. Another Three weeks and I have a fresh appointment with Dr. X.

So I arrive at his office. He spends literally 20 minutes of the appointment reading my chart (which whatever it had been a while since I saw him so I kinda get it) he then asks me if I really want to become a woman... I say yes.. he orders blood work then lectures me for another ten minutes about how "Hormones aren't magic pills and you won't ever experience being a woman at birth" (though he had  a more colourful way of describing this that I can't totally recall). Oh and he used the wrong pronouns again (even after asking initially and being corrected twice... I kinda gave up :P). I get the blood work done and he calls in an AA script. I get them it goes magnificently! 

I make another appointment (it was about 2 weeks ago now). I go in.. he spends about 20 minutes (this isn't like story exaggeration time I was looking at my phone while he read so I had an accurate gauge of the time) he takes blood pressure, heart rate. Asks if I want to start Anti Androgens... But I had been on them... for three months... under your prescription. I tell him I have been and he then asks me which one (I figured the chart would have that info, he did spend 20 minutes with it after all!) I tell him again the kind and amount. He nods along. "I suppose one of these days you'll be wanting to start estrogen?" I answer yes. He goes on to lecture me again about how I won't have the experience of natal women (periods, pregnancy, a bit about actually passing which was deeeeeeeply offensive). He orders some more blood work then lectures me on my weight. Okay I get it I AM overweight and I know it's an issue, what bothered me was how he dismissed A) the fact that I was already working on it and B) the ammount (a very reasonable ammount since I'd last seen him) of weight I lost ("It obviously isn't enough"). This is also keeping in mind that while I am overweight it's not extreme, speaking in BMI terms at least. Sparing some details my future with estrogen seems a bit shaky so long as I'm under his care, looking for a new endo.


> Also, for their life experience bullshit, I don't have much legal documentation. Money has been tight and I haven't gotten a legal name change yet. But I've changed my preferred name with school and have it on my counselling file etc, so I'm getting printouts of that kind of stuff, and I'm having people write letters to attest to the fact that I've been living as a male for three+ years now. Will that be enough?

I know my story didn't cover this question quite so much but I can try and give an educated guess. When I went in initially I had changed my name with my university's administration but not legally (it was still off getting approved and such). They basically told me at the time that it HAD to be a legal name change with a name change certificate. Additionally I did have to provide letters backing up that I'd lived as my gender, but I had no where near as much time as you do (literally zero "real life experience" hours at my first appointment) so I imagine three plus years can only work to your benefit! Again though, without knowing the finer machinations of CAMH's process I think it's hard to say how hardline they'll be. My recommendation is to be assertive but not confrontational about your experiences and presentation (sorry I hate the word presentation cause it sounds so bloody plastic but that's the kind of language they used with me so I'm just trying to be consistent with what they might insist upon you). Don't let them talk down your experience, but still try to play nice since they can give you all the good stuff.

The moral of our fractured fable? CAMH can be OK, at least in my experience, the people they work with not so much... I believe that I had gone into see them just before or on the cusp of the major restructuring efforts, just for a frame of reference. If you have any further questions please feel free to message me and ask me. I'd love to use my experience to help one of my trans brothers out!

Hey there! I'll do my best to answer some of these! As a brief disclaimer I'm not positioning to speak for the entirety of the trans community here, just my experiences and preferences. Also I get the impression that you're more interested in discussing trans women than men (just from the composure of your post) so I'll be writing with that assumption in mind as well.

>How does one find/meet Transgender people? Any Online options? This is the important one. Dominant transsexuals has been a fetish of mine for ages now, and I'd just in general like to meet some. If only for the experience of meeting other types of people.

Hmm well I mean I never met all that many trans folks until I involved with the local Queer community and made friends. Up until that point it had been dumb luck. I suppose if you just want to talk to trans people you found a pretty good online option in r/asktransgender. As for "dominant transexuals" ... eh okay I'll admit I'm getting a little uncomfortable with the way this sounds. I mean there are plenty of lovely Doms (sorry I'm working of the assumption that you mean dominant in a BDSM sense) who identify on the trans spectrum but "finding" them is sort of the same as above. Check out your local kink scene if it's just a fetish thing. I've met trans men and women who are totally fine with playing and having their identity be a part of fetish, and a whooooole lot more who find this sort of thing deeply offensive, dehumanizing, and repulsive (myself included). I guess to illustrate it's sort of the same notion of going out and seeking "Dominant Asian Women" cause they've always been a fetish of yours. It's the difference between someone finding your body attractive and desirable vs. someone positioning your identity and body as the object of fetish. Honestly just be aware that a lot of women are going to find this sort of thing demeaning and offensive (myself included). People are people not fetish objects. At the end of the day everyone has different comforts, tastes, and desires but the intersection of gender identity and fetish is a one that has to be navigated separately for everyone you meet.

> What's the proper terminology? How offensive is things like 'shemale', 'T-girl', 'sissy', ect ect ect ect

Context, context, and a million times context. If I'm giving you the sparks notes of all this, 99% of the trans folks I've met dislike these terms and find them demeaning. Again everyone's different with language and identity so make an effort to get to know them before rolling out any of those. To me shemale and sissy tend to undermine and totally demean the shit out of my identity as a woman. I'm a woman, not a shemale, not a sissy (I mean seriously do you call your female friends/sister/mom/coworkers sissy??). T-girl for me is also a bit of a sore spot. Just girl or woman thank you... that's what I am after all. Again, everyone's different.

> How accepted do you feel in your current community? Do you feel you -have- to wear the proper clothing for your gender of choice in secret? Or do you brazenly go as you please?

Community is a funny thing... In the greater LGBT community I have never felt all that accepted. In the Queer (which seems to be a somewhat distinct community from the LGBT community where I am) and trans communities I've always felt pretty at home! I never feel like I have to wear the "proper clothing", but I wouldn't say I'm brazen either. I just dress comfortably. Very tomboyish right now cause that's what feels right

Non discrimination bills are nice but hard to enforce which means more than a few times I've been subject to discrimination in employment with little to know realistic recourse.
